title: A Undertow for the Wardrobe
premise: Marguerite Eastwick, a translator who has spent a decade in a city that isn't his, learns that the crumbling house where he grew up—the one his family lost after his brother's trial—will be auctioned and demolished. Returning under the pretense of cataloguing its contents for the estate, he finds the house full of the borrowed words and buried testimonies he spent years translating away, including letters suggesting his brother took the blame for someone the town protected. As the auction approaches and the town's respectable families circle, Marguerite must choose between the safety of silence and a public reckoning that could cost him the last shreds of belonging. In the end, he reads his brother's letters aloud at the auction itself, forfeiting the bid but reclaiming the story, and leaves with nothing except the language he thought he'd lost.
about_author: Mara Dravenmoor is the pen name of a former court interpreter who spent eleven years translating testimony in coastal towns where everyone knew everyone and no one said anything. This is her second novel; the first was quietly withdrawn after a libel scare she now calls her apprenticeship.

chapters.title: The Grammar of Leaving
chapters.summary: Marguerite, translating a dull shipping contract in his rented flat, receives the auction notice for 14 Saltmere Row and misreads it three times before the words hold. POV: Marguerite, present day. Emotional beat: the numb shock of a past announcing itself in bureaucratic type.

chapters.title: Borrowed Words
chapters.summary: A flashback to childhood: the Eastwick house full of a hybrid home dialect—his grandmother's sea-words mixed with school English—and the night his older brother Tomas was arrested. POV: Marguerite, memory. Emotional beat: tenderness curdling into the first lesson in silence.

chapters.title: The Estate's Courtesy
chapters.summary: Marguerite contacts the auction house and talks his way into cataloguing the contents, telling himself it's about closure, not the letters he half-remembers. His editor warns him against going. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: self-deception dressed as professionalism.

chapters.title: Saltmere Row, Unlit
chapters.summary: He arrives in the town; the house stands boarded, and the first person to recognize him is the fishmonger's widow, who looks through him as if he were already a ghost. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: the vertigo of being a stranger in the place that made him.

chapters.title: Inventory of Small Betrayals
chapters.summary: Cataloguing the house room by room, Marguerite finds objects that testify—scratched doorframes, a hidden tin of letters—and realizes the auction will erase the only witness. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: grief sharpening into purpose.

chapters.title: What Tomas Carried
chapters.summary: First letter read: Tomas wrote from prison that he confessed to protect someone, and that the truth lived 'in the wardrobe of a house that drowns.' POV: Marguerite, with Tomas's letters in second voice. Emotional beat: the floor tilting—his brother's guilt was a translation too.

chapters.title: The Harrow Family at Church
chapters.summary: At Sunday service, Marguerite watches the Harrows—now the town's benefactors—endow a memorial wing, and notices the younger Harrow flinch at his brother's name in the hymnal margin. POV: Marguerite, observing. Emotional beat: suspicion arriving as a physical chill.

chapters.title: A Room Let to a Ghost
chapters.summary: Unable to afford lodging, Marguerite sleeps in the house itself, and the night sounds—the sea under the floorboards—begin speaking in his grandmother's dialect again. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: the house re-teaching him the language he'd surrendered.

chapters.title: The Widow's Ledger
chapters.summary: The fishmonger's widow, Edith, breaks her decade of silence: her husband saw something the night of the crime and died before he could say it, but he left a ledger of tide-times that contradicts the official timeline. POV: Edith, then Marguerite. Emotional beat: alliance formed over shared cowardice.

chapters.title: Justice, Off the Books
chapters.summary: Edith and Marguerite debate what justice means when the statute has expired and the guilty man funds the town's school roof. POV: alternating. Emotional beat: the seductive comfort of letting the law's silence stand.

chapters.title: The Demolition Date
chapters.summary: The auction house confirms demolition in three weeks; a developer's surveyor finds Marguerite squatting and serves him a trespass notice, and the town gossip machine ignites. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: exposure—the invisibility strategy failing on schedule.

chapters.title: Aunt Vess's Version
chapters.summary: His aunt, the last relative in town, gives her account: she always believed Tomas, but chose the family's survival over his name, and she begs Marguerite to do the same. POV: Aunt Vess. Emotional beat: love offered as a cage.

chapters.title: The Wardrobe Itself
chapters.summary: Marguerite finally opens the great wardrobe from his childhood and finds the rest of the letters plus a child's confession written in another boy's hand—young Aldous Harrow's. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: the terrible relief of proof.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Boathouse
chapters.summary: He confronts Aldous Harrow, now a magistrate, who neither denies nor confesses but offers money for the letters and the house's quiet demolition. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: rage discovering its own limits.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: Aldous's lawyer formalizes the offer—enough to buy the house outright, on condition the papers are burned. Marguerite imagines the life it could buy and hates how long he considers it. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: temptation as an honest mirror.

chapters.title: Edith's Condition
chapters.summary: Edith falls ill; from her hospital bed she tells him the ledger was never hers to keep quiet and that his brother once carried her husband home from the water. POV: Edith. Emotional beat: the dying releasing him from the pact of silence.

chapters.title: Translation, Finally Honest
chapters.summary: Marguerite spends a night translating Tomas's letters into plain school English, discovering that his professional skill was always an act of loyalty he'd mistaken for escape. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: vocation and reckoning becoming the same act.

chapters.title: Auction Day
chapters.summary: Bidders gather on the lawn; when the lot is called, Marguerite stands on the porch and reads Tomas's letters and the child's confession aloud, untranslated, in the old dialect and then in English. POV: Marguerite, with the crowd as chorus. Emotional beat: the climax—the private made public, at maximum cost.

chapters.title: The House Sells Anyway
chapters.summary: The reading changes nothing legal: the Harrow proxy buys the house, the crowd disperses in uncomfortable clusters, and Aldous resigns quietly by week's end. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: the anticlimax of real justice—partial, slow, unbought.

chapters.title: What the Demolition Leaves
chapters.summary: Watching the excavators, Marguerite retrieves the wardrobe's key from the rubble and gives the letters to the town archive, where Edith's ledger is finally filed beside them. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: inheritance redefined—what's kept is not property but record.

chapters.title: Undertow
chapters.summary: He swims at the old beach one last time and feels the pull his grandmother named, understanding at last that belonging is not staying but returning willingly. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: reconciliation with the sea, the town, and his own silence.

chapters.title: A Undertow for the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Back in the city, Marguerite accepts a translation of testimony—court work he'd always refused—and writes to Aldous in prison, offering the only inheritance left: the truth, in both languages. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: resolution—the art of almost saying it, ended for good.
